14339913B23556801435424: The region is a separate legal jurisdiction within an island union state: its own parliament, courts, prosecution service and police, with criminal justice devolved. The all-state framework above applies here in full — the biological-sex legal definition and the statutory single-sex services code bind here exactly as elsewhere in the state. What the region adds is machinery the other parts of the state lack: a dedicated transgender-identity aggravation in its hate-crime statute (in force since 2024) that is actually used — 104 charges carrying it in the latest year (up 21%) and 8,500+ hate crimes recorded in the act's first full year — so violence against trans people is named, charged and counted as its own category when a visitor reports it. The region's political culture is measurably more trans-accepting than the state average: a broader self-declaration gender-recognition law passed its parliament by a two-thirds majority in 2022 and was vetoed by the central government's first-ever use of an override power, later upheld in court — evidence of local intent, and of the state's power to negate it. Its prison agency's short-lived gender-identity custody policy was voided in a 2026 court ruling applying the state-wide sex definition, returning trans prisoners to birth-sex placement with no appeal; the rule of law here means that reversal is enforced, not optional. Two large cities have established trans communities and regular Pride events; survey opinion is the most supportive in the state. Complaints are processed; violence is treated as crime.
14339913B95766344400054: The union state's dominant region, with no devolved parliament or government: state law applies directly and most national institutions sit in its capital. Visitors stand under the full national framework with no local additions: the 2025 final-court biological-sex definition; the statutory single-sex services code in force August 2026 — administered by the state's equality watchdog from this region's capital, and the clearest 'you may be refused' signal on the map for toilets, gyms, hospital wards and refuges; a medicalised (and frozen) legal gender-recognition route; and — uniquely adverse for reporting — the state's hate-crime collection keeps no gender-identity strand among its five monitored categories, so anti-trans offending here is statistically invisible in official data even though 116,000 hate crimes were recorded across the monitored strands in the year to March 2025. No criminal penalty attaches to being trans or to gender expression; no arrest for presentation is documented. The region is simultaneously the map's best-documented counterweight and a contested public culture: its capital holds the country's largest visible scene, specialist services, a major annual Pride, active NGOs and litigation capacity, and its courts have convicted several documented attackers; yet organized street and hall confrontations with drag and trans-inclusive events have recurred in market towns, and church-and-media campaigns against 'gender ideology' are prominent in provincial life. Strong general rule of law; equality bodies litigate; protection is real but uneven between the capital and the shires.
14339913B89763821047858: A small devolved nation inside the union state, with its own parliament and government (since 1998) running education and public services — but no criminal law of its own, so the all-state framework stands: the 2025 biological-sex court settlement, the August 2026 statutory single-sex services code, and the same no-strand hate-crime collection as the state's dominant region. The regional contribution is posture rather than statute: its government has maintained an official LGBTQ+ action plan through the court ruling (standing update issued December 2025), has made statutory school guidance requiring schools to challenge harassment on gender-reassignment grounds and to record and monitor incidents, and prepared dedicated national guidance for trans pupils (consultation 2025) — a devolved administration publicly defending inclusion while the binding facility rules remain the state's. Two modest city scenes, an annual capital Pride, close community networks in a small, bilingual, chapel-and-rugby society where visibility is socially cheap to acquire and to lose. No provincial trans-specific incident series is documented; under-reporting is assumed rather than evidence of safety. Rule of law and complaint machinery function.
14339913B6930312138089: A separate legal jurisdiction inside the union state: its own courts, police service, assembly and justice ministry. Its criminal history is the state's harshest — male homosexuality was criminalised here until 2002, after the rest of the state decriminalised, and same-sex marriage arrived only in 2020, imposed by the central parliament over local refusal. Its police record a dedicated transgender-identity hate strand and the numbers rise; but assembly attempts to create a transgender sentencing aggravation stalled under the obstruction of the largest unionist party, so the region has the statistics without the charging tool its parliament debated. After the state's 2025 biological-sex ruling, the education minister removed the official transgender-pupils guidance — which had covered toilets and changing rooms in schools — from the web calling it unlawful and activist-made, while other parties press for its reinstatement; the power-sharing executive is split, with health ministers defending gender-service funding against the same party's campaigns. Documented sectarian-inflected intimidation: a pipe bomb thrown through the window of a trans woman's home in a border city (police classified it sectarian hate crime; she was displaced), earlier gun and arson attacks on queer venues; the capital's Pride proceeds under heavy police protection against organized counter-demonstrations. A small active scene, student visibility, functioning NGOs litigating through the region's courts, and equality bodies operating under direct-rule fallback. A close-knit, confessionally divided society where communal geography sets visibility risk: institutions respond, but society is not neutral.
